title: A crackme on a tiny virtual machine
description:
The capstone. The course provides a program for a small **virtual machine**, the kind of thing crackmes and CTF challenges use: a "licence check" that prints `OK` for a correct key and `NO` otherwise. You have its bytecode and, from reversing the interpreter, its instruction set. Build the tools, then use them to find every key it accepts.

**The machine**: eight 32-bit unsigned registers `r0`-`r7` (all 0 at the start), two flags `eq` and `lt` (false at the start), a program counter starting at 0, a read-only input string and an output string.

| Opcode | Bytes | Instruction | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `00` | 1 | `halt` | stop |
| `01` | 4 | `movi rA, imm16` | `rA = imm` (`01 A lo hi`) |
| `02` | 3 | `mov rA, rB` | `rA = rB` |
| `03` | 3 | `add rA, rB` | `rA += rB` |
| `04` | 3 | `sub rA, rB` | `rA -= rB` |
| `05` | 3 | `xor rA, rB` | `rA ^= rB` |
| `06` | 3 | `mul rA, rB` | `rA *= rB` |
| `07` | 4 | `andi rA, imm16` | `rA &= imm` |
| `08` | 3 | `cmp rA, rB` | `eq = rA == rB`, `lt = rA < rB` |
| `09` / `0A` / `0B` / `0C` | 3 | `jmp` / `je` / `jne` / `jl` addr16 | jump always / if `eq` / if not `eq` / if `lt` |
| `0D` | 3 | `in rA, rB` | `rA` = input character at index `rB`, or 0 past the end |
| `0E` | 2 | `out rA` | append the character `rA & 0xFF` to the output |

All arithmetic wraps at 32 bits; 16-bit values are little-endian.

```cpp
struct VmLine { std::uint16_t address; std::string text; };
struct VmResult { std::string output; bool halted; bool error; int steps; };

std::vector<VmLine> disassembleVm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& program);
VmResult runVm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& program, const std::string& input, int maxSteps);
std::vector<std::string> findKeys(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& program);
```

- **disassembleVm** works through the program from address 0. Texts: `halt`, `movi r0, 0x30`, `andi r0, 0xffff` (immediates in lowercase hex), `add r1, r7`, `jl 0x0065` (jump targets as four lowercase hex digits), `in r4, r1`, `out r6`. An unknown opcode, a register number above 7, or an instruction cut off by the end becomes `db 0xNN` for that one byte, and disassembly continues at the next.
- **runVm** executes. Every executed instruction, `halt` included, counts one step. It stops on `halt` (`halted` true), on an error (`error` true: an unknown opcode or bad register, an instruction running off the end of the program, or the program counter leaving the program), or after `maxSteps` steps (neither flag set).
- **findKeys** runs the program on every 4-digit input from `0000` to `9999` (with a limit of 10 000 steps) and returns, in order, those whose output is exactly `OK`.

Use your disassembler to read the program and understand the check before you brute-force it: the key space here is tiny, but the method of reading the bytecode is the point.
hints: Write one `fetch(program, address)` that decodes the instruction at an address into its opcode, register numbers, 16-bit value and length, or reports that it is not valid. The disassembler and the interpreter both use it, so they can never disagree about what an instruction is.

Read the listing before brute-forcing: the loop at `0x0014` reads four characters, rejects anything outside `0` to `9`, and mixes each into `r0` with `mul`, `xor` and `andi`; the result is compared with the constant loaded at `0x004E`. The brute force confirms what the reading tells you, and explains why there is more than one key.
requirements: The disassembler decodes every instruction and recovers from bad bytes.
The interpreter follows the specification exactly, including flags, wrapping and the input rules.
Errors and runaway programs are stopped cleanly.
stretch: Find the keys without brute force: run the hash backwards from the constant, digit by digit, and show why exactly two keys collide. Then change the program (with your own small assembler) so that only one key is accepted.
